title: Micro-slab admission flow for continuous batching and tail smoothing
creator: Aisha Khan
description:
Summary:
We observe persistent 95th/99th percentile tail latency spikes on mixed-length workloads during peak bursts. Investigation shows two dominant factors: (1) admission decisions bundle heterogeneous requests that lead to kernel path mismatch (long attention vs short attention kernels) and increase straggler probability, and (2) prefill/decode handoffs are not synchronized with kernel affinity, causing unnecessary context switches and KV cache thrash.

Proposal (Micro-slab admission flow):
- Slice incoming prefill requests into micro-slabs (sub-batches) keyed by predicted kernel path: attention width, sequence-length bucket, and quantization profile. Prediction uses lightweight histogram of recent seq-lengths + model metadata hints.
- Attach an urgency token to each micro-slab derived from SLA tier + observed queue wait time; tokens decay with age to favor older micro-slabs (age-based decay).
- Admission controller maintains a window of candidate micro-slabs and applies a slab-merging policy: merge compatible micro-slabs up to a kernel-capacity budget; otherwise schedule as isolated micro-batches to avoid stragglers.
- Integrate attention-prefetch hints into the prefill: scheduling prefetch for KV cache based on slab kernel affinity to reduce decode handoff latency.
- Add a kernel-affinity scorer that factors in expected runtime, memory pressure, and recent kernel tail variance; use scorer to bias slab merging and to select kernel variants (fast-approx vs exact).

Goals and success metrics:
- Reduce 95th/99th percentile latency by >=20% on mixed workloads (90% short, 10% long requests) under burst traffic compared to current baseline.
- Keep average throughput within 5% of baseline.
- No increase in token cost >3% for common workloads.

Plan of work:
1) Instrumentation (week 0-1): add lightweight seq-length predictor metrics, kernel path telemetry, and micro-slab lifecycle traces (enqueue, merge, dispatch, decode-handoff).
2) Prototype admission controller (week 1-2): implement micro-slab buckets + merge policy behind a feature flag. Local bench harness + synthetic mixed workload tests.
3) Kernel-affinity scorer & prefetch hints (week 2-3): server-side scorer and prefill hint plumbing to runtime.
4) Canary rollout (week 3-4): small percentage of traffic on dedicated infra with A/B dashboards and automatic rollback on regressions.
5) Gradual rollout + tuning (week 4-6): production rollout with telemetry-driven parameter tuning (slab size, merge thresholds, decay half-life).

Trade-offs considered:
- Micro-slabing increases metadata and scheduling overhead; we limit slab size and keep merge attempts bounded to control CPU cost.
- Aggressive merging can improve throughput but increases tail risk; the urgency token and kernel-affinity scorer aim to balance fairness and tail protection.
- Prefetching reduces latency but can increase memory pressure; we cap prefetched KV volume per slab and adaptively lower prefetch aggressiveness under memory pressure.

Rollout & rollback strategy:
- Feature flags at route/model level.
- Canary: 1% traffic on dedicated infra, monitor 95/99/Max latencies, qps, kernel-runway metrics.
- Automatic rollback triggers: 95th latency regression >10% for 5 minutes or kernel OOM events.

Documentation to create:
- Confluence: design doc with diagrams, state machine for micro-slab lifecycle, and tuning guide.
- Runtime README: configuration knobs.
acceptance_criteria: 95th-percentile latency reduced by >=20% on mixed (short+long) workload burst tests vs baseline
99th-percentile latency reduced by >=15% vs baseline without throughput regression
Throughput (tokens/s) within 5% of baseline for steady-state workloads
No kernel OOMs or increased memory-related errors in canary run
End-to-end smoke test script that validates slab creation, merge, dispatch, and prefetch behavior exists and passes

design_decisions: We prioritize tail-latency reduction over tiny average-case throughput gains for high-SLA customers; micro-slabs are size-limited to avoid CPU blowup. Kernel-affinity scorer is pluggable so future model-specific heuristics can be added without changing admission logic. Prefetching is conservative by default and governed by an adaptive budget to avoid regression on memory-bound nodes.
